answers.question: List of scenarios
answers.answer: The Society developed climate scenario analysis using three temperature scenarios: "Orderly" (1.5°C), "Too Little, Too Late" (>2°C), and "Hothouse" (>3°C).
answers.evidence: "We developed four climate scenario narratives, using conditions assumed to exist under three temperature scenarios: "Orderly", "Too Little, Too Late" and "Hothouse"." and from Appendix 2: "SCENARIOS: Orderly 1.5C | Too Little, Too Late >2C | Hothouse >3C"
answers.notes: The document mentions "four climate scenario narratives" but only three temperature scenarios are named. The four narratives likely refer to sub-scenarios within the three temperature bands, as described in the FSC sector scenarios framework.

answers.question: Global temperature outcome by 2100
answers.answer: The document describes three scenarios with different global temperature outcomes by 2100: (1) Orderly: 1.5°C warming (consistent with net zero by 2050); (2) Too Little, Too Late: 2.7°C warming; (3) Hothouse: 4.4°C warming.
answers.evidence: "This scenario is consistent with net zero by 2050, limiting global warming to 1.5 degrees C." / "Emissions decline steadily from 2020 to 2050 but, by 2050, are still higher than net zero. Globally temperatures warm by 2.7 degrees C by 2100." / "Ongoing fossil fuel use sees emissions continue to rise throughout the 21st century, leading to 4.4 degrees C of warming at the end of the century."
answers.location_hint: Appendix 1: FSC Climate Scenario Narratives, page 28
answers.notes: Three distinct scenarios are presented, each with a specific temperature outcome by 2100.

answers.question: Scenario provider
answers.answer: The Financial Services Council (FSC) provided the sector scenario narratives, and Finity Consulting Pty Ltd served as specialist external advisers to help create the scenarios.
answers.evidence: "Each scenario was created using conditions assumed to exist under each scenario, over three time-horizons (short, medium and long term), as described in the Climate Scenario Narratives for the Financial Services Sector report prepared by the Financial Services Council (dated 9 June 2023) (FSC sector scenarios)... Our scenarios were created with the help of specialist external advisers (Finity Consulting Pty Ltd), and with input from an internal working group made up of representatives from across the business (Society Working Group)."
answers.notes: The FSC provided the scenario framework/narratives, while Finity Consulting Pty Ltd provided specialist external advisory support in creating the scenarios.

answers.question: Pick-and-mix of SSPs and RCPs
answers.answer: Yes. The document uses a mix of SSPs and RCPs across different scenarios and purposes. For Global Climate Parameters: IPCC SSP1 (Orderly 1.5°C), IPCC SSP2 (Too Little, Too Late >2°C), and IPCC SSP3-7.0 (Hothouse >3°C). For NZ-specific Climate Parameters: NIWA RCP2.6 (Orderly), NIWA RCP4.5 (Too Little, Too Late), and NIWA RCP8.5 (Hothouse).
answers.evidence: SCENARIOS: Orderly 1.5C / Too Little, Too Late >2C / Hothouse >3C | Global Climate Parameters: IPCC SSP 1 / IPCC SSP2 / IPCC SSP3-7.0 | NZ-specific Climate Parameters: NIWA RCP2.6 / NIWA RCP4.5 / NIWA RCP8.5
answers.notes: The document explicitly uses SSPs for global climate parameters and RCPs for NZ-specific climate parameters, applying different frameworks at different geographic scales across the same three scenarios.

answers.question: Customised scenarios
answers.answer: No customised scenarios were developed. The Society used the Climate Scenario Narratives for the Financial Services Sector report prepared by the Financial Services Council (FSC, dated 9 June 2023) as a reference, adopting three temperature narratives: "Orderly", "Too Little, Too Late", and "Hothouse". No additional climate modelling was undertaken beyond that embedded in the FSC sector scenarios.
answers.evidence: "We used the Climate Scenario Narratives for the Financial Services Sector report prepared by the Financial Services Council (dated 9 June 2023) as a reference for the scenarios we created for our Climate Scenario Analysis. The three temperature narratives included in that report ("Orderly", "Too Little, Too Late" and "Hothouse") are summarised in the table below." and "We did not undertake any additional climate modelling beyond that which is embedded in the FSC sector scenarios."
answers.notes: The Society did not create customised scenarios from scratch; it adopted and applied the FSC sector scenarios directly.

answers.question: Co-produced climate scenarios
answers.answer: Yes. The Society co-produced its climate scenarios as a participant in the Financial Services Council (FSC) working group that developed the "Climate Scenario Narratives for the Financial Services Sector" report (dated 9 June 2023). The scenarios were also developed with the help of specialist external advisers (Finity Consulting Pty Ltd) and an internal Society Working Group made up of representatives from across the business.
answers.evidence: "The Society was a participant in the Financial Service Council working group that developed the scenarios and created the report. ... Our scenarios were created with the help of specialist external advisers (Finity Consulting Pty Ltd), and with input from an internal working group made up of representatives from across the business (Society Working Group)."
answers.notes: The FSC sector scenarios were used as the basis for the Society's four climate scenario narratives, covering three temperature scenarios ("Orderly", "Too Little, Too Late", and "Hothouse") over three time horizons.

answers.question: Baseline scenarios
answers.answer: The Society used three baseline scenarios: "Orderly" (1.5°C, aligned with IPCC SSP1, NGFS Net Zero 2050, IEA Net Zero by 2050, NIWA RCP2.6, CCC Tailwinds), "Too Little, Too Late" (>2°C, aligned with IPCC SSP2, NGFS Nationally Determined Contributions, IEA Announced Pledges Scenario Analysis, NIWA RCP4.5, CCC Headwinds), and "Hothouse" (>3°C, aligned with IPCC SSP3-7.0, NGFS Current Policies, IEA Stated Policies Scenario, NIWA RCP8.5, CCC Current Policy Reference). These were drawn from the FSC Climate Scenario Narratives for the Financial Services Sector (dated 9 June 2023).
answers.evidence: "SCENARIOS: Orderly 1.5C / Too Little, Too Late >2C / Hothouse >3C ... Global Climate Parameters: IPCC SSP 1 / IPCC SSP2 / IPCC SSP3-7.0 ... Global Emissions Pathways: NGFS Net Zero 2050 / IEA Net Zero by 2050 / NGFS Nationally Determined Contributions / IEA Announced Pledges Scenario Analysis / NGFS Current Policies / IEA Stated Policies Scenario ... NZ-specific Climate Parameters: NIWA RCP2.6 / NIWA RCP4.5 / NIWA RCP8.5 ... NZ-specific Emission Pathways: CCC Tailwinds / CCC Headwinds / CCC Current Policy Reference"
answers.notes: The scenarios were developed using the FSC Climate Scenario Narratives for the Financial Services Sector report (dated 9 June 2023) as a reference framework, with supporting data from IPCC, NGFS, IEA, NIWA, and CCC.

answers.question: Model used
answers.evidence: "In FY25 we implemented a new GHG data platform (Generate Zero) which enables us to record our GHG emissions with greater efficiency and accuracy. We worked with Generate Zero and their software to calculate our GHG emissions and prepare our GHG emissions inventory."
answers.notes: Generate Zero is the GHG data platform/software model used to calculate GHG emissions and prepare the GHG emissions inventory for FY25.

answers.question: Damage from acute physical risk considered
answers.answer: Yes. The Society considers damage from acute physical risks including business disruption due to extreme weather (storms, flooding, heat waves, and associated power blackouts), as well as monitoring claims following significant adverse weather events such as the Auckland Anniversary Weekend floods and Cyclone Gabrielle.
answers.evidence: "Business disruption due to extreme weather, including more storms, flooding and heat waves, with associated risks of power blackout. Limited impact in all three scenarios, over short to medium term. More likely in long term but still limited impact, noting that the Society does not cover emergency presentations. Short-term impacts on our business operations. For example, our ability to process claims and policies may be temporarily affected. Impacts are expected to be manageable, as part of our normal business continuity processes." and "We monitor our claims levels following any significant adverse weather events that occur. We assessed our claims levels following the Auckland Anniversary Weekend floods and Cyclone Gabrielle in 2023, and did not identify any material impact on claims or on the Society arising from those events."
answers.notes: The Society explicitly identifies acute physical risks (extreme weather events) and monitors claims following such events. The assessed impact is limited/manageable in the short to medium term across all scenarios.

answers.question: Non-temperature variables in scenarios
answers.answer: The scenarios include non-temperature variables such as: carbon pricing (emissions trading schemes and carbon taxes), regulatory/legislative changes (mandatory climate reporting, climate litigation), societal pressure and consumer preferences (towards low emission products), investment in low emission and emission abatement technology (e.g., electric vehicles, agricultural changes), electricity costs, price inflation across the economy, demographic and socio-economic changes, and extreme weather events (storms, flooding, heat waves, power blackouts).
answers.evidence:
"Progressive action across the globe supports a steady transition to a lower emissions economy. This includes greater stringency and scope of mandatory climate reporting, emissions trading schemes and carbon taxes around the world. Societal pressure is put on entities to decarbonise, with increasing climate litigation, and preferences change towards low emission products. Meanwhile, there is investment in low emission and emission abatement technology. This includes a rapid take up of electronic vehicles, and changes in the agricultural sector. Global emissions decline rapidly, driven in part by an increase in carbon pricing."

"In an Orderly future, where the NZ government is strongly encouraging a rapid conversion to almost complete use of renewable energy, cost pressures are significant because redundancy needs to be built into the system to guarantee supply. Pressure is not as great under a Too Little, Too Late future, but electricity costs still rise by 20% over the medium term. At the same time, the cost of raw materials increases, along with the cost of green waste disposal and gas capture, and there are increased costs associated with regulatory compliance."

"Business disruption due to extreme weather, including more storms, flooding and heat waves, with associated risks of power blackout."

"Complex mix of demographic and socio-economic changes, across the private and public health systems."

"Climate change contributes to price inflation across many sectors of the economy."
answers.notes: The scenarios are based on FSC Climate Scenario Narratives and include a range of non-temperature variables across the three scenarios (Orderly, Too Little Too Late, Hothouse). No single consolidated list of non-temperature variables is provided; they are described across multiple sections.

answers.question: Scale of scenarios
answers.answer: The Society used three temperature scenarios ("Orderly", "Too Little, Too Late", and "Hothouse") across three time horizons: Short Term (1-3 years), Medium Term (5-10 years), and Long Term (30+ years). The scenarios were developed using FSC Climate Scenario Narratives for the Financial Services Sector and cover global warming outcomes of approximately 1.5°C (Orderly), 2.7°C by 2100 (Too Little, Too Late), and 4.4°C by end of century (Hothouse).
answers.evidence: We developed four climate scenario narratives, using conditions assumed to exist under three temperature scenarios: "Orderly", "Too Little, Too Late" and "Hothouse". Each scenario was created using conditions assumed to exist under each scenario, over three time-horizons (short, medium and long term)... Time Horizons: Short Term 1-3 years (2025), Medium Term 5-10 years (2030), Long Term >30 years (2050+)
answers.notes: Four scenario narratives were developed under three temperature scenarios. The Orderly scenario is consistent with net zero by 2050 and limiting warming to 1.5°C; Too Little, Too Late results in 2.7°C warming by 2100; Hothouse results in 4.4°C warming by end of century.

answers.question: Justification for scenario/model choice
answers.answer: The Society used the Climate Scenario Narratives for the Financial Services Sector report prepared by the Financial Services Council (dated 9 June 2023) as the basis for its scenarios. This report was prepared to assist participants in the life insurance, health insurance and fund management sectors with climate scenario analysis, and the scenarios were therefore considered appropriate to the Society as a health insurer. Additionally, the Society was a participant in the Financial Services Council working group that developed the scenarios and created the report. Specialist external advisers (Finity Consulting Pty Ltd) and an internal working group also contributed to creating the scenarios.
answers.evidence: "We developed four climate scenario narratives, using conditions assumed to exist under three temperature scenarios: "Orderly", "Too Little, Too Late" and "Hothouse". Each scenario was created using conditions assumed to exist under each scenario, over three time-horizons (short, medium and long term), as described in the Climate Scenario Narratives for the Financial Services Sector report prepared by the Financial Services Council (dated 9 June 2023) (FSC sector scenarios). This report was prepared to assist participants in the life insurance, health insurance and fund management sectors with climate scenario analysis, and the scenarios were therefore considered appropriate to the Society, as a health insurer. The Society was a participant in the Financial Service Council working group that developed the scenarios and created the report."
answers.notes: The justification is explicitly stated: the FSC sector scenarios were designed for the life insurance, health insurance and fund management sectors, making them directly applicable to Southern Cross as a health insurer. The Society also had direct involvement in developing the scenarios through the FSC working group.

answers.question: Historic climate impacts
answers.answer: Southern Cross Medical Care Society did not identify any physical impacts of climate change on their business operations in the reporting period (FY25), with a quantified impact of zero. They also did not identify any impact on Members' claiming patterns attributable to climate-related events. The principal historic transitional impact was meeting obligations under the CRD (climate-related disclosure) regime, which impacted operating costs. Additionally, they assessed claims following the Auckland Anniversary Weekend floods and Cyclone Gabrielle in 2023 and did not identify any material impact on claims or on the Society from those events.
answers.evidence: "We did not identify any physical impacts of climate change on our business operations in the reporting period. The quantified impact is therefore zero. We did not identify any impact on our Members' claiming patterns that could be attributed to climate-related events in the reporting period. The principal transitional matter the Society was required to deal with in the FY25 reporting period was meeting our obligations under the CRD regime, impacting the Society's operating costs in the period." and "We assessed our claims levels following the Auckland Anniversary Weekend floods and Cyclone Gabrielle in 2023, and did not identify any material impact on claims or on the Society arising from those events. No significant adverse weather event occurred in the FY25 reporting period."
answers.notes: The document clearly states no physical climate impacts were identified in the reporting period, and no material claims impact from past weather events (Auckland floods and Cyclone Gabrielle in 2023). The only historic climate-related impact was transitional: costs associated with CRD compliance.

answers.question: Direct and indirect physical climate risks
answers.answer:
The Society identified two physical climate risks through its Climate Scenario Analysis:

1. **Claims inflation associated with rising temperatures** (particularly for individuals with co-morbidities): Limited impact over short and medium terms in all three scenarios; greater impact over long term in the Hothouse scenario. May require underwriting response or premium adjustments over the longer term.

2. **Business disruption due to extreme weather** (more storms, flooding and heat waves, with associated risks of power blackout): Limited impact in all three scenarios over short to medium term; more likely in long term but still limited impact (noting the Society does not cover emergency presentations). Short-term impacts on business operations (e.g., ability to process claims and policies) expected to be manageable through normal business continuity processes.

Overall, the Society considers it is unlikely to face material physical climate risks in the next 10 years. Over a 30-year period, assuming little or no progress towards limiting global temperature rise to 4°C (Hothouse scenario), rising temperatures in New Zealand could increase health insurance claims to a material extent.
answers.evidence: "Physical Risks: Claims inflation associated with rising temperatures, particularly for individuals with co-morbidities (for whom rising temperatures create greater health risks). Limited impact over short and medium terms, in all three scenarios. Greater impact over long term, in Hothouse scenario. Moderate increase in claims costs in some segments of our customer base. This may require an underwriting response or premium adjustments over the longer term. Business disruption due to extreme weather, including more storms, flooding and heat waves, with associated risks of power blackout. Limited impact in all three scenarios, over short to medium term. More likely in long term but still limited impact, noting that the Society does not cover emergency presentations. Short-term impacts on our business operations. For example, our ability to process claims and policies may be temporarily affected. Impacts are expected to be manageable, as part of our normal business continuity processes."
answers.notes: The document also notes on p.15 that "The Society is unlikely to face material physical climate risks in the next 10 years" and that over 30 years under a Hothouse scenario, rising temperatures could materially increase health insurance claims. No physical climate impacts were identified in the FY25 reporting period itself (p.16).
